claim: The warming-by-precipitation experiment was established in 2011 at the Haibei National Field Research Station of Alpine Grassland Ecosystem (37°37′N, 101°33′E, with elevation 3215 m), located on the northeastern Tibetan Plateau in Qinghai Province, China.
source: The warming-by-precipitation experiment was established in 2011 at the Haibei National Field Research Station of Alpine Grassland Ecosystem (37°37′N, 101°33′E, with elevation 3215 m), which is located on the northeastern Tibetan Plateau in Qinghai Province, China.
evidence: Direct statement from the Materials and methods section describing the experimental site location and establishment date.

claim: The climate type at the study site is continental monsoon with mean annual precipitation of 485 mm and annual average temperature approximately –1.7℃.
source: The climate type is a continental monsoon with mean annual precipitation of 485 mm and the annual average temperature approximately –1.7℃.
evidence: Direct statement providing climate data for the study site.

claim: High rainfall and temperature mainly occur in the peak-growing season from July to August at the study site.
source: The high rainfall and temperature mainly occur in the peak-growing season (from July to August Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Liu et al., 2018.

claim: The soils at the study site are Mat-Gryic Cambisols with an average pH value of surface soil (0–10 cm) being 6.4.
source: The soils are Mat-Gryic Cambisols, with the average pH value of surface soil (0–10 cm) being 6.4 (Ma et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement about soil characteristics supported by citation to Ma et al., 2017.

claim: The experimental design used a randomized block design with warming and altered precipitation treatments.
source: Briefly, experimental plots were established in an area of 50 m × 110 m in 2011, using a randomized block design with warming and altered precipitation treatments.
evidence: Direct statement describing the experimental design.

claim: The experiment included two levels of temperature: ambient temperature (T0) and elevated temperature of top 5 cm layer of the soil by 2℃ (T+).
source: Each block contained six plots (each plot was 1.8 m × 2.2 m), crossing two levels of temperature [ambient temperature (T0), elevated temperature of top 5 cm layer of the soil by 2℃ (T+)], and three levels of precipitation [natural precipitation (nP, represents ambient condition), 50% reduced precipitation (-P, represents 'drought' condition) and 50% enhanced precipitation (+P, represents 'wet' condition)].
evidence: Direct statement describing the temperature treatment levels.

claim: The experiment included three levels of precipitation: natural precipitation (nP), 50% reduced precipitation (-P, 'drought' condition), and 50% enhanced precipitation (+P, 'wet' condition).
source: Each block contained six plots (each plot was 1.8 m × 2.2 m), crossing two levels of temperature [ambient temperature (T0), elevated temperature of top 5 cm layer of the soil by 2℃ (T+)], and three levels of precipitation [natural precipitation (nP, represents ambient condition), 50% reduced precipitation (-P, represents 'drought' condition) and 50% enhanced precipitation (+P, represents 'wet' condition)].
evidence: Direct statement describing the precipitation treatment levels.

claim: Infrared heaters were suspended at 150 cm above the ground within each warming treatment plot.
source: In the warming treatments, two infrared heaters (1000 mm length, 22 mm width) were suspended in parallel at 150 cm above the ground within each plot.
evidence: Direct statement describing the warming treatment implementation.

claim: Rain shelters with V-shaped transparent polycarbonate resin channels were used to intercept 50% of incoming precipitation throughout the year in drought plots.
source: Four 'V'-shaped transparent polycarbonate resin channels (Teijin Chemical, Japan) were fixed at a 15° angle, above the infrared heaters, to intercept 50% of incoming precipitation throughout the year.
evidence: Direct statement describing the precipitation manipulation method.

claim: Collected rainfall from drought plots was supplied to wet plots manually after each precipitation event by sprinklers, increasing precipitation by 50%.
source: The collected rainfall from the drought plots was supplied to the wet plots manually after each precipitation event by sprinklers, increasing precipitation by 50%.
evidence: Direct statement describing how enhanced precipitation was achieved.

claim: Dummy infrared heaters and transparent polycarbonate resin channels were installed in control plots to control for shading effects.
source: To control for the effects of shading caused by infrared heaters, two 'dummy' infrared heaters and four 'dummy' transparent polycarbonate resin channels were installed in the control plots.
evidence: Direct statement describing the control for potential confounding effects.

claim: Each treatment had six replicates, resulting in thirty-six plots total.
source: Each treatment had six replicates, resulting in thirty-six plots.
evidence: Direct statement describing the experimental replication.

claim: Soil samples for qSIP incubation were collected in August 2020.
source: Soil samples for qSIP incubation were collected in August 2020.
evidence: Direct statement about sampling time.

claim: Three out of six plots were randomly selected as replicates for each treatment for the qSIP experiment.
source: Considering the cost of qSIP experiment (including the use of isotopes and the sequencing of a large number of DNA samples), we randomly selected three out of the six plots, serving as three replicates for each treatment.
evidence: Direct statement explaining the sampling strategy and justification.

claim: Three soil cores of topsoil (0–5 cm depth) were randomly collected and combined as a composite sample in each plot.
source: In each plot, three soil cores of the topsoil (0–5 cm in depth) were randomly collected and combined as a composite sample, which can be considered as a mixture of rhizosphere and bulk soils.
evidence: Direct statement describing the soil sampling method.

claim: The composite soil samples can be considered as a mixture of rhizosphere and bulk soils.
source: In each plot, three soil cores of the topsoil (0–5 cm in depth) were randomly collected and combined as a composite sample, which can be considered as a mixture of rhizosphere and bulk soils.
evidence: Direct statement characterizing the nature of the soil samples.

claim: Fresh soil samples were sieved (2 mm) to remove root fragments and stones.
source: The fresh soil samples were shipped to the laboratory and sieved (2 mm) to remove root fragments and stones.
evidence: Direct statement describing soil sample processing.

claim: Soil samples from ambient temperature treatments were air-dried at 14℃ (average temperature across the growth season).
source: Soil samples of ambient temperature treatments (including T0-P, T0nP, and T0 +P) were air-dried at 14℃ (average temperature across the growth season), while the soil samples of warming treatments (including T+-P, T+nP, and T++P) were air-dried at 16℃ (increased temperature of 2℃).
evidence: Direct statement describing the incubation temperature for ambient treatment samples.

claim: Soil samples from warming treatments were air-dried at 16℃ (increased temperature of 2℃).
source: Soil samples of ambient temperature treatments (including T0-P, T0nP, and T0 +P) were air-dried at 14℃ (average temperature across the growth season), while the soil samples of warming treatments (including T+-P, T+nP, and T++P) were air-dried at 16℃ (increased temperature of 2℃).
evidence: Direct statement describing the incubation temperature for warming treatment samples.

claim: Air-dried soils (2.00 g) were incubated with 400 μl of 98 atom% H218O (18O treatment) or natural abundance water (16O treatment) in the dark for 2 days.
source: We incubated the air-dried soils (2.00 g) with 400 μl of 98 atom% H218O (18O treatment) or natural abundance water (16O treatment) in the dark for 2 d by using sterile glass aerobic culture bottles (Diameter: 29 mm; Height: 54 mm).
evidence: Direct statement describing the incubation procedure.

claim: A total of 54 soil samples were collected, including 18 pre-wet samples and 36 incubation samples.
source: A total of 54 soil samples, including 18 pre-wet samples (6 treatments × 3 replicates) and 36 incubation samples (6 treatments × 3 replicates × 2 types of H2O addition), were collected.
evidence: Direct statement quantifying the total number of samples.

claim: Total DNA from all collected soil samples was extracted using the FastDNA SPIN Kit for Soil according to the manufacturer's instructions.
source: Total DNA from all the collected soil samples was extracted using the FastDNA SPIN Kit for Soil (MP Biomedicals, Cleveland, OH, USA) according to the manufacturer's instructions.
evidence: Direct statement describing the DNA extraction method.

claim: Mechanical cell destruction was attained by multi-size beads beating at 6 m s–1 for 40 s.
source: Briefly, the mechanical cell destruction was attained by multi-size beads beating at 6 m s–1 for 40 s, and then FastDNA SPIN Kit for Soil (MP Biomedicals, Cleveland, OH, USA) was used for DNA extraction.
evidence: Direct statement describing the cell lysis procedure.

claim: All DNA samples were extracted by the same person within 2–3 hours using a unifying procedure of cell lysis and DNA extraction.
source: All DNA samples were extracted by the same person within 2–3 hr, and a unifying procedure of cell lysis and DNA extraction was used.
evidence: Direct statement describing standardization of the extraction procedure.

claim: DNA concentration was determined fluorometrically using Qubit DNA HS Assay Kits on a Qubit 4 fluorometer.
source: The concentration of extracted DNA was determined fluorometrically using Qubit DNA HS (High Sensitivity) Assay Kits (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) on a Qubit 4 fluorometer (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA).
evidence: Direct statement describing the DNA quantification method.

claim: 3 μg DNA were added into 1.85 g ml–1 CsCl gradient buffer with a final buoyant density of 1.718 g ml–1 for isopycnic centrifugation.
source: Briefly, 3 μg DNA were added into 1.85  g ml–1 CsCl gradient buffer (0.1 M Tris-HCl, 0.1 M KCl, 1 mM EDTA, pH = 8.0) with a final buoyant density of 1.718  g ml–1.
evidence: Direct statement describing the isopycnic centrifugation setup.

claim: Ultracentrifuge tubes were spun at 177000 g at 18℃ for 72 hours with minimum acceleration and braking.
source: All tubes were spun in an Optima XPN-100 ultracentrifuge (Beckman Coulter) using a VTi 65.2 rotor at 177000  g at 18℃ for 72  h with minimum acceleration and braking.
evidence: Direct statement describing the ultracentrifugation conditions.

claim: The contents of each ultracentrifuge tube were separated into 20 fractions (~250 μl each fraction) after centrifugation.
source: Immediately after centrifugation, the contents of each ultracentrifuge tube were separated into 20 fractions (~250  μl each fraction) by displacing the gradient medium with sterile water at the top of the tube using a syringe pump (Longer Pump, LSP01‐2 A, China).
evidence: Direct statement describing the fractionation procedure.

claim: The buoyant density of each fraction was measured using a digital hand-held refractometer from 10 μl volumes.
source: The buoyant density of each fraction was measured using a digital hand-held refractometer (Reichert, Inc, Buffalo, NY, USA) from 10 μl volumes.
evidence: Direct statement describing the density measurement method.

claim: Fractionated DNA was precipitated from CsCl by adding 500 μl 30% polyethylene glycol (PEG) 6000 and 1.6 M NaCl solution, incubated at 37℃ for 1 hour and then washed twice with 70% ethanol.
source: Fractionated DNA was precipitated from CsCl by adding 500  μl 30% polyethylene glycol (PEG) 6000 and 1.6 M NaCl solution, incubated at 37℃ for 1 hr and then washed twice with 70% ethanol.
evidence: Direct statement describing the DNA precipitation and washing procedure.

claim: The DNA of each fraction was dissolved in 30 μl of Tris‐EDTA buffer.
source: The DNA of each fraction was then dissolved in 30  μl of Tris‐EDTA buffer.
evidence: Direct statement describing the final DNA resuspension.

claim: Total 16S rRNA gene copies for DNA samples of all fractions were quantified using primers 515F and 907R for V4-V5 regions.
source: Total 16S rRNA gene copies for DNA samples of all the fractions were quantified using the primers for V4-V5 regions: 515F (5′‐GTG CCA GCM GCC GCG G‐3′) and 907R (5′‐CCG TCA ATT CMT TTR AGT TT‐3′) (Guo et al., 2018).
evidence: Direct statement describing the qPCR primers used, supported by citation.

claim: The V4-V5 primer pairs were chosen to facilitate integration and comparison with data from previous studies.
source: The V4-V5 primer pairs were chosen to facilitate integration and comparison with data from previous studies (Ruan et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Direct statement explaining the rationale for primer selection, supported by citations.

claim: Plasmid standards were prepared by inserting a copy of purified PCR product from soil DNA into Escherichia coli.
source: Plasmid standards were prepared by inserting a copy of purified PCR product from soil DNA into Escherichia coli.
evidence: Direct statement describing the preparation of qPCR standards.

claim: Average PCR efficiency was 97% and the average slope was –3.38, with all standard curves having R2 ≥ 0.99.
source: Average PCR efficiency was 97% and the average slope was –3.38, with all standard curves having R2 ≥ 0.99.
evidence: Direct statement reporting qPCR performance metrics.

claim: The DNA of pre-wet soil samples and fractionated DNA of fractions with buoyant density between 1.703 and 1.727 g ml–1 (7 fractions) were selected for 16S rRNA gene sequencing.
source: The DNA of pre-wet soil samples (unfractionated) and the fractionated DNA of the fractions with buoyant density between 1.703 and 1.727 g ml–1 (7 fractions) were selected for 16S rRNA gene sequencing by using the same primers of qPCR (515F/907R).
evidence: Direct statement describing which fractions were sequenced.

claim: The fractions with density between 1.703 and 1.727 g ml–1 were selected because they contained more than 99% gene copy numbers of each sample.
source: The fractions with density between 1.703 and 1.727 g ml–1 were selected because they contained more than 99% gene copy numbers of each sample.
evidence: Direct statement explaining the rationale for fraction selection.

claim: A total of 270 DNA samples were sequenced using the NovaSeq6000 platform.
source: A total of 270 DNA samples [18 total DNA samples of prewet soil +252 fractionated DNA samples (6 treatments × 3 replicates × 2 types of water addition × 7 fractions)] were sequenced using the NovaSeq6000 platform (Genesky Biotechnologies, Shanghai, China).
evidence: Direct statement quantifying the number of samples sequenced and the platform used.

claim: Raw sequences were quality-filtered using USEARCH v.11.0.
source: The raw sequences were quality-filtered using the USEARCH v.11.0 (Edgar, 2010).
evidence: Direct statement describing the sequence processing software, supported by citation.

claim: Sequences < 370 bp and total expected errors > 0.5 were removed during quality filtering.
source: Sequences < 370 bp and total expected errors > 0.5 were removed.
evidence: Direct statement describing quality filtering parameters.

claim: High-quality sequences were clustered into operational taxonomic units (OTUs) at a 97% identity threshold.
source: Subsequently, high-quality sequences were clustered into operational taxonomic units (OTUs) with 'cluster_otus' commandat a 97% identity threshold, and the most abundant sequence from each OTU was selected as a representative sequence.
evidence: Direct statement describing OTU clustering method.

claim: The taxonomic affiliation of representative sequences was determined using the RDP classifier (version 16).
source: The taxonomic affiliation of the representative sequence was determined using the RDP classifier (version 16) (Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: Direct statement describing taxonomic classification method, supported by citation.

claim: In total, 19,184,889 reads of the bacterial 16S rRNA gene and 6,938 OTUs were obtained.
source: In total, 19,184,889 reads of the bacterial 16S rRNA gene and 6,938 OTUs were obtained.
evidence: Direct statement reporting sequencing output.

claim: The sequences were uploaded to the National Genomics Data Center (NGDC) Genome Sequence Archive (GSA) with accession numbers CRA007230.
source: The sequences were uploaded to the National Genomics Data Center (NGDC) Genome Sequence Archive (GSA) with accession numbers CRA007230.
evidence: Direct statement providing data availability information.

claim: 18O labeling occurs during cell growth via DNA replication.
source: As 18O labeling occurs during cell growth via DNA replication, the amount of 18O incorporated into DNA was used to estimate the growth rates of active taxa.
evidence: Direct statement explaining the principle of 18O-qSIP method.

claim: The amount of 18O incorporated into DNA was used to estimate the growth rates of active taxa.
source: As 18O labeling occurs during cell growth via DNA replication, the amount of 18O incorporated into DNA was used to estimate the growth rates of active taxa.
evidence: Direct statement describing how growth rates were estimated.

claim: The density shifts of OTUs between 16O and 18O treatments were calculated following the qSIP procedures.
source: The density shifts of OTUs between 16O and 18O treatments were calculated following the qSIP procedures (Hungate et al., 2015; Koch et al., 2018).
evidence: Direct statement describing the calculation method, supported by citations.

claim: An exponential growth model was assumed over the course of the incubations.
source: We assumed an exponential growth model over the course of the incubations.
evidence: Direct statement describing the growth model assumption.

claim: Collectively, 1373 OTUs were identified as '18O incorporators' (i.e. OTUs with growth rates significantly greater than zero).
source: Collectively, 1373 OTUs were identified as '18O incorporators' (i.e. OTUs with growth rates significantly greater than zero) and used for subsequent data analyses.
evidence: Direct statement reporting the number of OTUs with detectable growth.

claim: The maximum cumulative growth rates of the whole communities occurred in the ambient temperature and ambient precipitation condition (T0nP).
source: The maximum cumulative growth rates of the whole communities occurred in the ambient temperature and ambient precipitation condition (T0nP), and all climate manipulations had negative effects on soil bacterial growth (Figure 3A).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 3A showing growth rates across treatments.

claim: All climate manipulations had negative effects on soil bacterial growth.
source: The maximum cumulative growth rates of the whole communities occurred in the ambient temperature and ambient precipitation condition (T0nP), and all climate manipulations had negative effects on soil bacterial growth (Figure 3A).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 3A showing reduced growth under all treatments.

claim: The individual impact of warming, drought, and wet conditions resulted in the most substantial negative effects on bacterial growth compared with the combined effects of warming × drought and warming × wet.
source: The individual impact of warming, drought, and wet conditions resulted in the most substantial negative effects on bacterial growth compared with the combined effects of warming × drought and warming × wet.
evidence: Direct statement comparing single versus combined effects.

claim: The antagonistic interactions between warming and modified precipitation patterns were observed.
source: The individual impact of warming, drought, and wet conditions resulted in the most substantial negative effects on bacterial growth compared with the combined effects of warming × drought and warming × wet. A result that illustrates the antagonistic interactions between warming and modified precipitations patterns (Figure 3B).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 3B showing interaction effects.

claim: The combined effect size of wet and warming was smaller than that of drought and warming, indicating a higher degree of antagonism of warming × wet.
source: Moreover, the combined effect size of wet and warming was smaller than that of drought and warming, indicating a higher degree of antagonism of warming × wet.
evidence: Direct statement comparing the degree of antagonism between scenarios.

claim: Growth of the major bacterial phyla was negatively influenced by the individual climate factors.
source: Growth of the major bacterial phyla was also negatively influenced by the individual climate factors (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 3C and D showing phylum-level growth responses.

claim: The antagonistic interactions of T and P were prevalent among the major phyla (except Bacteroidetes showed the additive interaction between drought and warming).
source: The antagonistic interactions of T and P were prevalent among the major phyla (except Bacteroidetes showed the additive interaction between drought and warming).
evidence: Direct statement describing interaction patterns at the phylum level.

claim: Significant smaller combined effect sizes of warming × wet were found in the major phyla compared with that of warming × drought (p < 0.05), such as Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes and Betaproteobacteria, indicating higher degree of antagonism.
source: We also found the significant smaller combined effect sizes of warming × wet in the major phyla compared with that of warming × drought (p < 0.05), such as Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes and Betaproteobacteria, indicating higher degree of antagonism.
evidence: Direct statement reporting statistical comparison of effect sizes.

claim: In Actinobacteria and Bacteroidetes, the effect of wet and warming neutralized each other, as the combined effect of these two factors had no effect on growth.
source: In Actinobacteria and Bacteroidetes, the effect of wet and warming neutralized each other, as the combined effect of these two factors had no effect on growth.
evidence: Direct statement describing neutralizing effects in specific phyla.

claim: Warming (T+nP) reduced the growth of 75% of the taxonomic groups.
source: The single-factor effects on the growth of incorporators tended to be negative (Figure 4B): Warming (T+nP) reduced the growth of 75% of the taxonomic groups, which was followed by drought and wet (74% and 67%, respectively).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4B quantifying the proportion of taxa negatively affected.

claim: Drought reduced the growth of 74% of the taxonomic groups.
source: The single-factor effects on the growth of incorporators tended to be negative (Figure 4B): Warming (T+nP) reduced the growth of 75% of the taxonomic groups, which was followed by drought and wet (74% and 67%, respectively).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4B quantifying the proportion of taxa negatively affected.

claim: Wet conditions reduced the growth of 67% of the taxonomic groups.
source: The single-factor effects on the growth of incorporators tended to be negative (Figure 4B): Warming (T+nP) reduced the growth of 75% of the taxonomic groups, which was followed by drought and wet (74% and 67%, respectively).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4B quantifying the proportion of taxa negatively affected.

claim: Warming × drought and warming × wet had smaller impacts on the growth of incorporators compared with the single effects (especially T++P, only 43% of incorporators showed negative growth responses).
source: Warming × drought and warming × wet had the smaller impacts on the growth of incorporators, compared with the single effects (especially T++P, only 43% of incorporators showed negative growth responses).
evidence: Direct statement comparing combined versus single effects with quantification.

claim: The interaction type of T and P on the growth of ~70% incorporators was antagonistic.
source: The interaction type of T and P on the growth of ~70% incorporators was antagonistic (i.e. the combined effect size is smaller than the additive expectation) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 4C quantifying the prevalence of antagonistic interactions.

claim: The weak antagonistic interaction on bacterial growth was dominant under the warming × drought conditions (41% of incorporators).
source: The weak antagonistic interaction on bacterial growth was dominant under the warming × drought conditions (41% of incorporators), while more incorporators (34%) whose growth subjected to neutralizing effect was found under the warming × wet conditions.
evidence: Direct statement quantifying the proportion of taxa showing weak antagonistic interactions.

claim: More incorporators (34%) whose growth subjected to neutralizing effect was found under the warming × wet conditions.
source: The weak antagonistic interaction on bacterial growth was dominant under the warming × drought conditions (41% of incorporators), while more incorporators (34%) whose growth subjected to neutralizing effect was found under the warming × wet conditions.
evidence: Direct statement quantifying the proportion of taxa showing neutralizing effects.

claim: The findings were robust at a subOTUs level by the zero-radius OTU (ZOTU) analysis.
source: These findings were robust at a subOTUs level by the zero-radius OTU (ZOTU) analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement supported by supplementary figures showing consistency of results.

claim: The most incorporators whose growth was influenced by the antagonistic interaction of T and P showed significant phylogenetic clustering (NTI > 0, p < 0.05).
source: Overall, the most incorporators whose growth was influenced by the antagonistic interaction of T and P showed significant phylogenetic clustering (i.e. species clustered at the phylogenetic branches, indicating close genetic relationship; NTI > 0, p < 0.05).
evidence: Direct statement reporting phylogenetic analysis results with statistical significance.

claim: The incorporators whose growth subjected to the additive interaction of warming × drought showed significant phylogenetic clustering (p < 0.05).
source: The incorporators whose growth subjected to the additive interaction of warming × drought also showed significant phylogenetic clustering (p < 0.05), but randomly distributed under warming × wet scenario (p = 0.116).
evidence: Direct statement reporting phylogenetic clustering with statistical significance.

claim: The incorporators whose growth subjected to the additive interaction of warming × wet were randomly distributed (p = 0.116).
source: The incorporators whose growth subjected to the additive interaction of warming × drought also showed significant phylogenetic clustering (p < 0.05), but randomly distributed under warming × wet scenario (p = 0.116).
evidence: Direct statement reporting random phylogenetic distribution with p-value.

claim: Incorporators whose growth is influenced by the synergistic interaction of T and P showed random phylogenetical distribution under both climate scenarios (p > 0.05).
source: In addition, incorporators whose growth is influenced by the synergistic interaction of T and P showed random phylogenetical distribution under both climate scenarios (p > 0.05).
evidence: Direct statement reporting random phylogenetic distribution with statistical threshold.

claim: Higher overall antagonistic intensity of warming × wet than that of warming × drought was found, contributing by a higher proportion of incorporators whose growth subjected to neutralizing effect.
source: We found higher overall antagonistic intensity of warming × wet than that of warming × drought, contributing by a higher proportion of incorporators whose growth subjected to neutralizing effect (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement supported by figures comparing antagonistic intensities.

claim: Of the total 1373 incorporators, 1218 were shared in both warming × drought and warming × wet scenarios.
source: Of the total 1373 incorporators, 1218 were shared in both warming × drought and warming × wet scenarios (Figure 5A).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 5A showing overlap of taxa.

claim: The difference in interactive effects between warming × drought and warming × wet was due to a within-species change in growth response (i.e. phenotypic plasticity of organisms), rather than changes in species composition (i.e. species sorting).
source: That is, the difference in interactive effects between warming × drought and warming × wet we observed was due to a within-species change in growth response (i.e. phenotypic plasticity of organisms), rather than changes in species composition (i.e. species sorting).
evidence: Direct statement interpreting the overlap data as evidence for phenotypic plasticity.

claim: Of the species identified in both scenarios, 453 incorporators were assigned a higher degree of antagonistic interaction of warming × wet than that of warming × drought.
source: Of these species identified in both warming × drought and warming × wet scenarios, 453 incorporators were assigned a higher degree of antagonistic interaction of warming × wet than that of warming × drought.
evidence: Direct statement quantifying taxa with differential antagonism.

claim: The growth of 215 incorporators were influenced by the weak antagonistic interaction of warming × drought, and neutralizing effect of warming × wet.
source: Further, the growth of 215 incorporators were influenced by the weak antagonistic interaction of warming × drought, and neutralizing effect of warming × wet.
evidence: Direct statement identifying a specific subset of taxa with particular interaction patterns.

claim: The growth response of 215 species could contribute mainly to the overall growth patterns observed in grassland bacterial community under warming and altered precipitation scenarios, because of the prevalence of weak antagonistic interaction of warming × drought and neutralizing effect of warming × wet.
source: The growth response of these 215 species could contribute mainly to the overall growth patterns observed in grassland bacterial community under warming and altered precipitation scenarios, because of the prevalence of weak antagonistic interaction of warming × drought and neutralizing effect of warming × wet (Figure 4C).
evidence: Direct statement inferring the importance of these taxa based on their prevalence and interaction patterns.

claim: The top three OTUs with the highest growth rates possessed extremely high species abundance.
source: The top three OTUs with the highest growth rates possessed extremely high species abundance (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Direct statement supported by source data showing abundance information.

claim: The member affiliated to Solirubrobacter (OTU 14) has high functional potential for aerobic C fixation and CO oxidation, nitrogen assimilation and assimilatory nitrite to ammonia, and phosphatase synthesis and phosphate transport transport-related functions.
source: The three taxa also possessed a higher functional potential related to carbon (C), nitrogen (N), sulfur (S), and phosphorus (P) cycling: the member affiliated to Solirubrobacter (OTU 14), has the high functional potential for aerobic C fixation and CO oxidation, nitrogen assimilation and assimilatory nitrite to ammonia, and phosphatase synthesis and phosphate transport transport-related functions.
evidence: Direct statement describing predicted functional potential based on PICRUSt2 analysis.

claim: The members affiliated to the genus Pseudonocardia (OTU 5 and OTU 31) harbor a higher functional potential for aerobic C fixation, aerobic respiration, and CO oxidation, dissimilatory nitrate to nitrite and nitrogen assimilation, and sulfur mineralization functions.
source: The members affiliated to the genus Pseudonocardia (OTU 5 and OTU 31), harbor a higher functional potential for aerobic C fixation, aerobic respiration, and CO oxidation, dissimilatory nitrate to nitrite and nitrogen assimilation, and sulfur mineralization functions.
evidence: Direct statement describing predicted functional potential based on PICRUSt2 analysis.

claim: OTU 14 (Solirubrobacter) was predicted to have larger genomes and proteomes.
source: Furthermore, we annotated the genomic characteristics by aligning species sequences to the GTDB database (Genome Taxonomy Database), and we found that OTU 14 (Solirubrobacter) was predicted to have larger genomes and proteomes (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Direct statement reporting genomic predictions based on GTDB alignment.

claim: These three species could play essential roles at the species and functional levels of ecosystems.
source: All these results suggested that these three species could play essential roles at the species and functional levels of ecosystems.
evidence: Direct statement inferring ecological importance based on growth rates and functional potential.

claim: After a decade of temperature and precipitation regime shift, the pervasive negative impacts of climate factors on soil bacterial growth in alpine grassland ecosystem were observed.
source: After a decade of temperature and precipitation regime shift, the pervasive negative impacts of climate factors on soil bacterial growth in alpine grassland ecosystem were observed (Figure 3), which supports our first hypothesis that long-term warming and altered rainfall events consistently reduce microbial growth.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing the main finding and relating it to the hypothesis.

claim: A 15-year warming study reduced the growth rate of soil bacteria in a montane meadow in northern Arizona.
source: Consistent with our findings, a recent experimental study demonstrated that 15 years of warming reduced the growth rate of soil bacteria in a montane meadow in northern Arizona (Purcell et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement citing another study with consistent findings.

claim: The negative effects of climate factors on microbial growth are likely due to the variation related to availability of soil moisture and organic carbon.
source: These negative effects of climate factors on microbial growth are likely due to the variation related to availability of soil moisture and organic carbon (Dieleman et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: Direct statement proposing a mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: Warming has a negative impact on soil carbon pools.
source: Previous evidences suggest that warming has a negative impact on soil carbon pools (Jansson and Hofmockel, 2020; Purcell et al., 2022), mainly because of the rapid soil carbon mineralization and respiration (Melillo et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement citing previous evidence for warming effects on carbon pools.

claim: Warming causes rapid soil carbon mineralization and respiration.
source: Previous evidences suggest that warming has a negative impact on soil carbon pools (Jansson and Hofmockel, 2020; Purcell et al., 2022), mainly because of the rapid soil carbon mineralization and respiration (Melillo et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement explaining the mechanism of carbon pool reduction, supported by citation.

claim: The reduction of microbially accessible carbon pools may explain the diminished microbial growth after long-term warming.
source: Carbon is the critical element in cell synthesis, the reduction of microbially accessible carbon pools may explain the diminished microbial growth after long-term warming.
evidence: Direct statement proposing a mechanistic explanation based on carbon limitation.

claim: Long-term warming can induce soil water deficiency, thereby slowing microbial growth.
source: In addition, long-term warming can induce soil water deficiency (Dieleman et al., 2012; Jansson and Hofmockel, 2020), thereby slowing microbial growth.
evidence: Direct statement proposing another mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: As soil water availability is reduced, changes in osmotic pressure cause microbial death or dormancy, while others can accumulate solutes to survive under lower water potentials.
source: As soil water availability is reduced, changes in osmotic pressure cause microbial death or dormancy, while others can accumulate solutes to survive under lower water potentials (Schimel, 2018).
evidence: Direct statement describing microbial responses to water stress, supported by citation.

claim: Accumulation of osmolytes could depend on highly energetic expenses, resulting in less energetic allocation to growth (trade-offs between microbial growth and physiological maintenance).
source: However, such accumulation of osmolytes could depend on highly energetic expenses (Boot et al., 2013; Jansson and Hofmockel, 2020; Schimel et al., 2007), resulting in less energetic allocation to growth (trade-offs between microbial growth and physiological maintenance).
evidence: Direct statement explaining the energetic trade-off, supported by citations.
